question.en:
Select the idiom that best expresses the given meaning.

Completely confused and unsure about what to do

solution_text.en:
Meaning: at sea = completely confused; not knowing what to do (असमंजस में, उलझन में)

Example: On her first day in the accounts section, Priya was at sea with the new software.

Why the others are wrong.

• At large = (of a criminal) not yet caught, free (फ़रार); also 'as a whole' (society at large).

• At bay = held off, kept at a distance (दूर रखा हुआ), as in keep the disease at bay.

• At odds = in disagreement (असहमति में), as in the two partners were at odds over the budget.

Origin. A sailor far out at sea, with no land in sight, could easily lose his bearings. The phrase moved from being lost on the water to being lost in thought.

All four start with 'at'; only 'sea' carries the picture of being lost with no shore in sight.

option_1.en: To criticise Nepal for failing to prepare for the recent floods despite repeated warnings

option_2.en: To explain the scientific causes of the recent floods and of the swelling of glacial lakes

option_3.en: To back Nepal's call for climate justice but warn that words need money and institutions

option_4.en: To argue that India and China, as Nepal's largest neighbours, alone should pay for its recovery

question.en:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

When Nepal's Prime Minister, Balendra Shah, rose to address the UN General Assembly for the first time, he did not ask the world for pity. He asked it to look at a ledger. The floods that recently tore through his country left at least 1,400 people dead and more than 6,000 missing, and rebuilding is expected to cost about a tenth of the nation's GDP. Nepal, meanwhile, is responsible for less than 0.1 per cent of the greenhouse gases the world releases. To call this merely a natural disaster, he suggested, is to miss the point; it is a question of climate justice.

The argument deserves support. A poor country that spends its scarce money on repairing bridges and rehousing families is, by the same act, spending less on schools, clinics and jobs. Every rupee consumed by recovery is a rupee withdrawn from development. This is precisely why the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities exists: every nation must act, but those who have polluted most and can afford most must carry more of the load.

Nor is this Nepal's concern alone. The Himalayan watersheds pay no attention to borders. The rivers that rise in Nepal flow on to water Indian farms and turn Indian turbines, and China has its own stake in the same mountains. Cooperation, therefore, is not charity but enlightened self-interest. Nepal's proposal for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, which would bring Nepal, India and China together to share satellite data, monitor glacial lakes, issue early warnings and respond jointly to disasters, gives that interest a practical shape.

Still, fine speeches have a short shelf life. Climate diplomacy can easily decay into a ritual in which leaders express sympathy, pass resolutions and go home without committing any money. Demands for compensation, however just, will remain slogans unless there are workable ways to decide who owes what and to get funds to the people who need them. The real test of Mr Shah's appeal, then, will not be the applause it drew in New York. It will be whether money and working institutions are ready before the next flood arrives, rather than another round of speeches once it has passed.

What is the author's main purpose in writing the passage?

solution_text.en:
The author supports the appeal:

"The argument deserves support."

and then warns:

"The real test… will be whether money and working institutions are ready before the next flood arrives, rather than another round of speeches once it has passed."

So the purpose is support + caution.

Why the others are wrong.

• Criticise Nepal: the author never blames Nepal, and no earlier warnings are mentioned; the passage takes its side.

• Scientific causes: glacial lakes are mentioned only as something to monitor; the passage discusses justice, cooperation and finance, not the science of floods.

• India and China alone should pay: the author says cooperation serves their interest; it never asks them alone to pay. Responsibility lies with "those who have polluted most".

Answer: To back Nepal's call for climate justice but warn that words need money and institutions

Word help.

• ledger (बही-खाता; हिसाब)

• climate justice (जलवायु न्याय)

According to the passage, which of the following is NOT one of the functions of the proposed Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism?

solution_text.en:
The passage lists the functions:

"…which would bring Nepal, India and China together to share satellite data, monitor glacial lakes, issue early warnings and respond jointly to disasters…"

Hydropower is mentioned only as an Indian interest ("turn Indian turbines"), not as a task of the mechanism.

Why the others are wrong.

• Sharing satellite data across borders: listed (the data is shared among Nepal, India and China).

• Monitoring glacial lakes in the region: listed.

• Issuing early warnings of disasters: listed.

Answer: Building joint hydropower projects

Word help.

• glacial lake (हिमनद झील)

• turbine (टरबाइन; बिजली बनाने वाला घूमने वाला यंत्र)

• watersheds (जलग्रहण क्षेत्र)

In a NOT question, tick off each option against the list; the odd one is often a word borrowed from a nearby line.

Why does the author describe cooperation over the Himalayas as 'not charity but enlightened self-interest'?

solution_text.en:
The lines just before the phrase give the reason:

"The Himalayan watersheds pay no attention to borders. The rivers that rise in Nepal flow on to water Indian farms and turn Indian turbines, and China has its own stake in the same mountains."

Helping Nepal manage these shared rivers also protects India's farms and power, and China's interests. Helping others for one's own good = enlightened self-interest.

Why the others are wrong.

• Nepal will repay once its economy recovers: no promise of repayment is mentioned.

• Charity between nations not permitted: the principle is about sharing duties by capacity and past pollution; it says nothing about forbidding charity.

• India and China caused the damage: the passage blames global emissions, not these two neighbours.

Answer: Because India and China would also gain from protecting the rivers and mountains they share with Nepal

Word help.

• enlightened self-interest (प्रबुद्ध स्वार्थ; दूसरों की भलाई में अपना हित देखना)

• stake (हिस्सेदारी, हित)

Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word 'scarce' as used in the passage.

solution_text.en:
"A poor country that spends its scarce money on repairing bridges…"

Scarce = available only in small amounts; not enough (दुर्लभ, कम). A poor country has little money to spare.

Opposite → plentiful = available in large amounts (प्रचुर, भरपूर).

Why the others are wrong.

• Insufficient = not enough (अपर्याप्त): same meaning as scarce — the synonym trap.

• Prosperous = rich and successful (समृद्ध, संपन्न): opposes 'poor', the word describing the country, not 'scarce'. It describes a person or nation; 'prosperous money' makes no sense.

• Sacred = holy (पवित्र): look-alike of scarce, unrelated meaning.

Answer: Plentiful

Word help.

• rehousing (फिर से बसाना)

• differentiated (भिन्न-भिन्न, अलग-अलग तय किया हुआ)

Which of the following statements is TRUE according to the passage?

solution_text.en:
The passage says:

"Demands for compensation, however just, will remain slogans unless there are workable ways to decide who owes what and to get funds to the people who need them."

'Decide who owes what' = fix who owes what; 'get funds to the people' = deliver funds. Option is true.

Why the others are wrong.

• Option is false: "he did not ask the world for pity"; he framed it as climate justice.

• Option is false: "every nation must act"; the richest polluters must only carry more of the load, not act alone.

• Option is not given: the mechanism is only a proposal; nothing is said about India or China agreeing to fund it.

Answer: The author believes compensation claims need workable ways to fix who owes what and to deliver funds.

question.en:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom highlighted in bold in the given sentence.

After the factory shut down, Ravi took up two part-time jobs just to make ends meet.

solution_text.en:
Meaning: make ends meet = to earn or have just enough money to pay for one's basic expenses (किसी तरह गुज़ारा चलाना)

Ravi lost his regular job, so he needed two part-time jobs only to cover his daily expenses.

Why the others are wrong.

• become rich very quickly through a lucky business deal: the sentence shows hardship (तंगी), not sudden wealth.

• finish every task well before the final deadline: 'ends' here are not the ends of a task; no deadline is mentioned.

• settle a quarrel between two old friends: 'meet' does not mean bringing people together here.

Origin. Usually traced to book-keeping: the 'ends' are the two totals of an account, income and spending; making them meet means the money coming in just covers the money going out.

Word help. shut down (बंद हो जाना)

Make ends meet = income just covers expenses; it signals a struggle, never comfort.

solution_text.en:
The passage welcomes the 2047 target but argues that it must be reached by a cheaper and cleaner path. The closing line sums it up:

"…the industry will be judged not by the tonnes it can produce but by whether it can make steel more cheaply, more cleanly and higher up the value chain."

So the title must carry both ideas: a big target and a better route.

Why the others are wrong.

Answer: A Big Steel Target Needs a Cleaner, Cheaper Route

solution_text.en:
The passage states it directly:

"Since raw materials account for 65 to 70 per cent of the cost of making steel, a bigger import bill is not a side issue…"

Why the others are wrong.

• About 92 per cent is the share of coking coal that is imported, not the share of cost.

• Roughly 7 per cent is the assumed annual GDP growth.

• Less than one-third is not mentioned anywhere.

Answer: 65 to 70 per cent

Word help.

• crude steel (कच्चा इस्पात)

• coking coal (कोकिंग कोयला; इस्पात बनाने में प्रयुक्त कोयला)

• side issue (गौण मुद्दा)

option_1.en: cost far more to build than new plants that run on scrap, renewable electricity or hydrogen

option_2.en: violate the European Union's carbon border tax, which now bars carbon-intensive steel from European ports

option_3.en: leave its biggest cost item dependent on imported coal and weaken its access to markets that price emissions

option_4.en: push up domestic coal prices sharply as India's own coking coal reserves run out over the coming decades

solution_text.en:
Two separate lines have to be joined.

Line 1: "Roughly 92 per cent of the coking coal it uses is already imported… Since raw materials account for 65 to 70 per cent of the cost of making steel, a bigger import bill… goes to the heart of the business."

→ The biggest cost item would depend even more on foreign supply.

Line 2: "The furnace route is also carbon-intensive, and the European Union's carbon border tax now links access to its market with the emissions embedded in every tonne…"

→ Dirtier steel would find it harder to enter markets that price emissions.

Only Option combines both risks.

Why the others are wrong.

• Option reverses the passage. It is the scrap, renewable and hydrogen routes that "may look costly today"; it never says the furnace route costs more to build.

• Option overstates the tax. The tax links market access to emissions; the passage does not say it bars steel from European ports.

• Option invents a cause. The passage says the coal is imported; it says nothing about India's own reserves running out or domestic coal prices rising.

Answer: leave its biggest cost item dependent on imported coal and weaken its access to markets that price emissions

Word help.

• carbon-intensive (अधिक कार्बन उत्सर्जन करने वाला)

• embedded (अंतर्निहित, भीतर समाया हुआ)

• contradiction (विरोधाभास)

In inference questions, reject any option that adds a fact (reserves) or strengthens a word (links → bars).
